newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Metals-Zinc seen higher, focus also on lead.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals-Zinc seen higher, focus also on lead.

text.p: Far East base metals traders focused on zinc on Friday as talk circulated of a squeeze being engineered by a big trading house and as prices hovered close to seven-year highs of $1,500 a tonne.
A rally in lead saw traders switching attention to that metal as fund buying and short covering pushed prices to their highest level since early April.
Lead on the London Metal Exchange (LME) broke above $640, peaking at $657 a tonne early Friday and eyeing $670.
"Chinese producers have been frustrated with lead prices recently but it should have gone through the bottom already," a trader in Singapore said.
"Breaking $650 is quite instructive but it is fund buying not fundamentals so it could be short-lived," she said.
Far East selling had been seen on Thursday, she said.
Lead premiums basis cargo and freight (C&F) in Singapore were around $28 a tonne over LME cash, another trader said.

Premiums on Chinese zinc made by small factories were at a huge discount to the LME cash prices, traders said, with one Hong Kong source saying the non-registered metal was being offered at $1,200 a tonne.
The cost of producing a tonne of zinc metal in China was around $1,000, she said.
While some South Asian customers were happy to take the Chinese metal, delivery was a problem, with some Vietnamese customers having waited two months past the due date for their orders to arrive.
"It meets the Chinese national export quality standard, so there is no problem with the quality, it's just that delivery is a real problem," she said.
LME zinc has gained around $150 in the past week, with last trade on Thursday at $1,476 a tonne and with an expectation it would break $1,500 on Friday.
Premiums on LME-registered Chinese zinc brands such as Torch, produced by the Zhuzhou smelter, were around $70-80 a tonne, traders in Hong Kong, Singapore and China said.
An official of the Zhuzhou smelter denied the factory, one of China's major zinc makers and exporters, was short in the market as rumours for the past few months had suggested.
He said a potential dispute with Swiss trade house Glencore over the quality of 100 tonnes of Torch zinc had been resolved.
He also denied market talk the smelter had cranked up production to 110-120 percent over annual capacity of 250,000 tonnes to meet the rumoured short positions.
Market talk had indicated Zhuzhou was among the victims of an engineered squeeze.
Zhuzhou executives have said production has been at a peak as the smelter moves to take advantage of the current good prices.
Traders in Asia and Australasia said they expected Chinese authorities to move to cap zinc exports to prevent any tightening of supply in the domestic market, which could have an inflationary effect.
One analyst in Sydney suggested the Beijing government could re-impose an export tax that had been removed on January 1 this year.
Other said exports were more likely to be restricted by a lack of new export licences. Zhuzhou has export rights, Huludao and other requires licences.
Tolling, however, would keep these factories ticking over and remain a source of revenue, the traders said.
Official figures show China's exports of unwrought zinc and zinc alloys reached 198,386 tonnes in the first five months of 1997, a rise of 129.3 percent compared with the year-ago period.
--Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6441
